subject: biology

items.q: Which statement correctly describes how new cells are generated in a living organism?
items.correct: A parent cell divides to produce two daughter cells, and everything the parent contained is shared out between them.
items.misconception: A parent cell produces two daughter cells and then goes on living alongside them as a third cell.
items.why: The words 'mother cell' and 'daughter cells' suggest a human family, in which the mother goes on living after her children are born. A parent cell divides to produce two daughter cells. Everything the parent cell contained is shared between the two daughters; no parent cell remains.
items.specStatementText: New cells only come from cells dividing
items.random_wrong: A parent cell splits at one moment into many small daughter cells, which then grow to full size in the tissue.

items.q: How does cytokinesis in an animal cell differ from cytokinesis in a plant cell?
items.correct: An animal cell is pinched in two by a ring of actin and myosin; a plant cell builds new membrane and wall from vesicles at its equator.
items.misconception: Both cells are pinched in two by a contractile ring, but in a plant cell the ring acts more slowly because it must squeeze the wall as well.
items.why: At GCSE and MYP level cytokinesis is described for all cells as 'the cytoplasm and cell membrane divide', and the only diagram most students have seen is the animal cell pinching in two. Only animal cells are pinched in two by a contractile ring of actin and myosin. A plant cell cannot be pinched because of its rigid wall; instead vesicles assemble a cell plate of new membrane and wall at the equator, from the inside outwards.
items.specStatementText: Cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm, differently in animals and plants
items.random_wrong: An animal cell is pinched in two by spindle microtubules; a plant cell builds new membrane and wall from vesicles at its equator.

items.q: A dividing cell is examined after its two new nuclei have formed. Many small vesicles are seen gathering and fusing in a line across the equator of the cell, midway between the nuclei. Which conclusion is justified?
items.correct: It is a plant cell: the vesicles are assembling sections of new membrane and cell wall to separate the daughter cells.
items.misconception: It is a plant cell: the vesicles carry enzymes that soften the existing wall so that it can grow inwards across the cell.
items.why: Students know the plant cell cannot pinch because the wall is rigid, and they adapt the animal 'furrow from the outside' model by making the wall itself do the furrowing. The direction is the reverse of the animal cell. Vesicles fuse at the equator into a cell plate, which enlarges outwards until it joins the existing wall; the old wall plays no active part.
items.specStatementText: Cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm, differently in animals and plants
items.random_wrong: It is a plant cell: the vesicles mark the line along which the cell membrane will be pinched inwards to split the cytoplasm.

items.q: Which statement about the division of the cytoplasm between two daughter cells is correct?
items.correct: Each daughter cell must receive at least one mitochondrion, because mitochondria form only by division of existing ones.
items.misconception: The cytoplasm is divided equally in every cell division, so that each daughter cell receives exactly half of each type of organelle.
items.why: Every diagram of mitosis and meiosis shows two identical daughter cells, and the phrase 'genetically identical daughter cells' is heard as 'identical daughter cells'. Division of the cytoplasm is usually equal, but not in every case. In human oogenesis the oocyte keeps almost all the cytoplasm and a tiny polar body is produced; in yeast a small bud is pinched off a much larger parent cell.
items.specStatementText: Cytokinesis is usually equal, but not always
items.random_wrong: A daughter cell that receives no mitochondria can synthesize new ones from proteins made on its ribosomes, so none need be shared.

items.q: In human oogenesis, the first meiotic division produces a large secondary oocyte and a very small polar body. What does this unequal cytokinesis achieve?
items.correct: The oocyte keeps almost all the cytoplasm and organelles for the future zygote, while both cells receive a complete haploid set of chromosomes.
items.misconception: The oocyte receives a larger share of the chromosomes along with the extra cytoplasm, so the polar body has fewer chromosomes to be discarded.
items.why: Students conflate the size of a cell with the amount of everything in it, and picture 'unequal division' as a single unequal split of the whole cell, nucleus included. Nuclear division and cytokinesis are separate processes. The nucleus divides first and each daughter nucleus receives a full set of chromosomes; the cytoplasm is then divided, equally or unequally. In oogenesis the tiny polar body has the same chromosome number as the large oocyte.
items.specStatementText: Cytokinesis is usually equal, but not always
items.random_wrong: The polar body is the result of a failed equal division; in normal oogenesis the cytoplasm is divided equally between two egg cells of equal size.

items.q: Which statement correctly compares the roles of mitosis and meiosis in eukaryotes?
items.correct: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number and genome of the cell the same, whereas meiosis halves the chromosome number and generates diversity.
items.misconception: Mitosis keeps the full set of genes in each cell, whereas meiosis produces cells that carry only half of the organism's genes.
items.why: 'Halves the genetic material' and 'half the chromosomes' are compressed to 'half the genes'; students picture the genome being cut in two rather than the two sets being separated. Meiosis separates the two chromosome sets of a diploid nucleus. Each haploid nucleus receives one chromosome of every homologous pair, so it carries every gene once. Halving the chromosome number does not remove any genes.
items.specStatementText: Mitosis keeps the genome; meiosis halves it and adds variety
items.random_wrong: Mitosis doubles the chromosome number, which meiosis then halves, so together the two processes keep the number constant.

items.q: Nuclear division normally occurs before the cytoplasm of a cell is divided. What would result if a cell divided its cytoplasm into two without first dividing its nucleus?
items.correct: One daughter cell would be anucleate: with no chromosomes it could not transcribe genes to replace its proteins or divide again.
items.misconception: Each daughter cell would build itself a new nucleus from the DNA and proteins present in its share of the cytoplasm.
items.why: Students think of the nucleus as an organelle that the cell can make, like a ribosome, rather than as the structure that holds the chromosomes, which exist only as copies of previous chromosomes. Nuclear division is needed before cell division to avoid the production of anucleate cells. The chromosomes must be replicated and shared out by mitosis or meiosis; a daughter cell that received no nucleus would have no genome.
items.specStatementText: Mitosis keeps the genome; meiosis halves it and adds variety
items.random_wrong: Both daughter cells would receive a nucleus, because DNA replication has already doubled the number of chromosomes to provide two sets.

items.q: What is the structure of a chromosome after DNA replication and before anaphase?
items.correct: Two identical elongated DNA molecules, the sister chromatids, held together at the centromere.
items.misconception: Two DNA molecules, one inherited from each parent, joined together to form a homologous pair.
items.why: Diagrams show a replicated chromosome as an X made of two arms, and students who have learned that 'one comes from each parent' attach that fact to the only pair they can see. Sister chromatids are produced by DNA replication and are genetically identical. Homologous chromosomes are separate chromosomes that carry the same genes but may have different alleles; they are not joined together, except temporarily as a bivalent in meiosis I.
items.specStatementText: DNA is replicated once before either division
items.random_wrong: A single elongated DNA molecule, which is not copied to form a second chromatid until prophase.

items.q: A cell of an organism has 8 chromosomes before its DNA is replicated. How many chromosomes and how many DNA molecules are in its nucleus at metaphase of mitosis?
items.correct: 8 chromosomes, 16 DNA molecules
items.misconception: 16 chromosomes, 16 DNA molecules
items.why: The word 'copy' suggests two chromosomes, and counting the arms of an X-shaped diagram gives two; students also assume that if the DNA has doubled the chromosome count must have doubled. After replication each chromosome consists of two elongated DNA molecules (chromatids) held together until anaphase, but it is still counted as one chromosome. A human cell has 46 chromosomes throughout interphase and until anaphase, when the separated chromatids become 92 chromosomes for a moment before the cell divides.
items.specStatementText: DNA is replicated once before either division
items.random_wrong: 8 chromosomes, 8 DNA molecules

items.q: How is the DNA of a eukaryotic chromosome condensed before nuclear division?
items.correct: The DNA is wound around histone proteins, and the fibre so formed is supercoiled into a much shorter, thicker structure.
items.misconception: The double helix itself twists ever more tightly, with no proteins involved, until the molecule is short enough to be seen.
items.why: The DNA helix is already described as a coil, so 'supercoiling' is heard as 'more of the same coiling' rather than as coiling of a DNA–protein fibre. Condensation depends on histones: DNA winds around histone proteins to form nucleosomes, and this DNA–protein fibre is then coiled and supercoiled. The naked double helix could not be packed into a chromosome on its own.
items.specStatementText: Chromosomes condense and are moved by microtubules in both divisions
items.random_wrong: The DNA is already packed as a condensed chromosome throughout the cycle; staining at division merely makes it visible.

items.q: In both mitosis and meiosis, chromosomes are moved to the poles of the cell during anaphase. What causes this movement?
items.correct: Microtubule motor proteins move the chromosomes along spindle microtubules, which shorten as the chromosomes travel.
items.misconception: The spindle microtubules contract in the same way as muscle fibres, pulling the chromosomes towards the poles.
items.why: Textbooks say the spindle fibres 'pull' the chromatids apart, and the only pulling fibre most students know is a contracting muscle fibre. Microtubules are rigid tubes that lengthen and shorten by adding or removing subunits; they cannot contract. Chromosome movement uses microtubule motor proteins that move along the microtubules, which shorten as the chromosome approaches the pole.
items.specStatementText: Chromosomes condense and are moved by microtubules in both divisions
items.random_wrong: The separated chromatids repel one another and so drift apart to opposite ends of the cell without any attachment.

items.q: Which statement about the phases of mitosis in a human cell is correct?
items.correct: In anaphase, the sister chromatids of each chromosome are separated and moved to opposite poles.
items.misconception: In anaphase, the two chromosomes of each homologous pair are separated and moved to opposite poles.
items.why: Meiosis is taught soon after mitosis, and the striking image of homologous pairs separating is transferred back to mitosis; the phrase 'chromosomes separate' is used loosely for both. Mitosis maintains the chromosome number, so both chromosomes of every homologous pair must go to each daughter cell. What separates in anaphase of mitosis is the pair of identical chromatids of each chromosome. Homologous chromosomes are separated only in meiosis I.
items.specStatementText: The four phases of mitosis
items.random_wrong: In metaphase, the chromosomes line up at the equator while still enclosed within the nuclear envelope.

items.q: A parent cell with 46 chromosomes divides by mitosis. Why are the two daughter cells genetically identical to each other and to the parent cell?
items.correct: Every chromosome was replicated into two identical chromatids before division, and one chromatid of every chromosome goes to each daughter cell.
items.misconception: Each daughter cell receives half of the parent cell's 46 chromosomes and then replicates them to restore the full set of 46.
items.why: 'Division' means halving in everyday use, and students who have not tracked replication assume each daughter must get half. The DNA is replicated before mitosis, so the parent cell has two copies of every DNA molecule. Anaphase sends one chromatid of each chromosome to each pole, so each daughter cell receives the full chromosome number and the whole genome, identical to the parent.
items.specStatementText: The four phases of mitosis
items.random_wrong: Each daughter cell receives one chromosome from each of the 23 homologous pairs, and both chromosomes of a pair carry the same genes.

items.q: Two cells are seen in a stained micrograph of a root tip. Cell 1 has an intact nucleus in which no separate chromosomes can be distinguished. Cell 2 has no nuclear envelope, and its condensed chromosomes lie in a single line across the middle of the cell. Which identification is correct?
items.correct: Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in metaphase.
items.misconception: Cell 1 is in prophase; cell 2 is in metaphase.
items.why: Cell-cycle diagrams put interphase in the same wheel as the phases of mitosis, and 'the first thing you see' in a sequence of micrographs is an interphase nucleus, so it is taken to be the first phase. Interphase is the period between nuclear divisions and is not a phase of mitosis. Prophase is identified by condensed, visible chromosomes and the disappearance of the nuclear envelope. Most cells in a growing tissue are in interphase.
items.specStatementText: Reading the phase from a diagram or micrograph
items.random_wrong: Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in prophase.

items.q: A student counted 100 cells in a micrograph of a growing root tip. 85 cells had an intact nucleus with no visible chromosomes; 6 had condensed chromosomes scattered through the cell; 3 had chromosomes aligned across the equator; 4 had two groups of chromatids moving apart; 2 had two groups of chromosomes at the poles with nuclear envelopes forming. Which conclusion is correct?
items.correct: About 15% of the cells are in mitosis, and prophase is the most frequent phase among the dividing cells.
items.misconception: Nine of the cells are in metaphase, because scattered and aligned condensed chromosomes both lie in the middle of the cell.
items.why: Students identify metaphase by position ('middle of the cell') rather than by alignment, and a mass of condensed chromosomes in prophase is usually in the middle of the cell. The criterion for metaphase is alignment of the chromosomes on one plane at the equator of the spindle. Condensed chromosomes lying in a disordered mass, even if central, show a cell in prophase.
items.specStatementText: Reading the phase from a diagram or micrograph
items.random_wrong: All 100 cells are in mitosis, because the 85 with an intact nucleus and no visible chromosomes are in prophase.

items.q: A diploid nucleus of an organism with 2n = 14 undergoes meiosis. What is produced?
items.correct: Four haploid nuclei, each containing 7 chromosomes
items.misconception: Four diploid nuclei, each containing 14 chromosomes
items.why: The rule 'replicate, then divide' is learned for mitosis and is applied to each division of meiosis separately. There is a single replication before meiosis I. Because meiosis II separates chromatids that already exist, without further replication, the four nuclei produced each have half the chromosome number of the original diploid nucleus.
items.specStatementText: Meiosis: two divisions, one diploid nucleus to four haploid
items.random_wrong: Four haploid nuclei, each with half of the organism's genes

items.q: Which statement correctly outlines the two rounds of segregation in meiosis?
items.correct: In meiosis I the two chromosomes of each homologous pair separate; in meiosis II the sister chromatids of each chromosome separate.
items.misconception: In meiosis I the sister chromatids of each chromosome are separated, and in meiosis II the homologous chromosomes of each pair are separated.
items.why: Mitosis is learned first and involves separation of chromatids, so students assume the first division of meiosis is 'the same as mitosis' and the reduction happens second. The reduction happens in the first division: bivalents separate in anaphase I so that each nucleus has one chromosome of each pair, each still made of two chromatids. Meiosis II then separates the chromatids, producing four haploid nuclei.
items.specStatementText: Meiosis: two divisions, one diploid nucleus to four haploid
items.random_wrong: In meiosis I the homologous chromosomes are separated; the DNA is then replicated so that meiosis II can separate the new chromatids.

items.q: Why is meiosis needed in a sexual life cycle?
items.correct: Fertilization combines the chromosomes of two gametes, so the number must be halved beforehand to keep it constant across generations.
items.misconception: Gametes could be produced by mitosis instead, because when two diploid gametes fuse the zygote they form is diploid like its parents.
items.why: Students see fertilization as two cells 'joining' and do not track the chromosomes; 'diploid plus diploid gives diploid' feels natural because the parents and offspring are all diploid. Fertilization fuses two nuclei and combines their chromosomes. In a sexual life cycle the number must therefore be halved by meiosis at some stage, so that fusion restores, rather than doubles, the diploid number.
items.specStatementText: Meiosis: two divisions, one diploid nucleus to four haploid
items.random_wrong: Each gamete must carry only half of the parent's genes, so that the offspring gets one half from each parent and no gene is duplicated.

items.q: A child has Down syndrome. Both parents have 46 chromosomes in each of their body cells. Which statement about the origin of the condition in this child is correct?
items.correct: One parent produced a gamete with 24 chromosomes because chromosome 21 failed to separate in meiosis, so the zygote had 47 chromosomes.
items.misconception: A mutation in the zygote altered the base sequence of one gene on chromosome 21, so the child carries a faulty allele of that gene.
items.why: Down syndrome is described as a 'genetic condition', and in the genetics course genetic conditions are usually caused by mutant alleles of single genes. Down syndrome is used as an example of an error in meiosis. The genes on chromosome 21 are normal; the problem is that three copies of the whole chromosome are present because of non-disjunction, giving 47 chromosomes per cell.
items.specStatementText: Non-disjunction and Down syndrome
items.random_wrong: The extra chromosome 21 was produced at fertilization, when the nuclei of a normal sperm and a normal egg fused and their chromosomes combined.

items.q: Which statement about crossing over is correct?
items.correct: Non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange lengths of DNA, producing new combinations of alleles.
items.misconception: Sister chromatids of one chromosome exchange lengths of DNA, so that the two chromatids come to differ from each other.
items.why: The sister chromatids are the pair that students can see joined together in diagrams, and 'chromatids exchange segments' is remembered without the word 'non-sister'. Crossing over takes place in prophase I between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes. Sister chromatids are identical, so exchanging DNA between them would produce no new combination; exchange between homologues combines alleles from the two parents on one chromatid.
items.specStatementText: Meiosis makes variation: random orientation and crossing over
items.random_wrong: The exchange of DNA alters the base sequence at the exchanged region, creating new alleles of the genes found there.

items.q: A species has a diploid number of 8. Ignoring crossing over, how many different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes can random orientation of bivalents produce in its gametes?
items.correct: 16, because each of the 4 bivalents can be oriented in 2 ways, independently of the others
items.misconception: 8, because each of the 4 bivalents contributes 2 possible orientations to the total
items.why: Students treat each bivalent as contributing two possibilities to a running total instead of multiplying, or count the pairs themselves as the combinations, or they substitute the diploid number for the number of pairs because it is the number given. Independent events multiply: 2 × 2 × 2 … for n bivalents is 2ⁿ. For humans, with 23 pairs, this is 2²³, over 8 million combinations, which is why 2 × 23 = 46 is far too small.
items.specStatementText: Meiosis makes variation: random orientation and crossing over
items.random_wrong: 256, because each of the 8 chromosomes can be oriented in 2 ways, independently of the others

items.q: Which pair of examples correctly matches cell proliferation to its role?
items.correct: Cells in the meristems of a plant dividing: growth; cells beneath the surface of the skin dividing: routine replacement of cells shed from the surface.
items.misconception: Cells throughout the stem and leaves of a plant dividing: growth; cells in an early-stage animal embryo dividing: repair of damage to the embryo.
items.why: Animal growth is met first and in an early embryo every cell divides, so the same picture is applied to plants. In plants, cell proliferation for growth is confined to meristems. Cells produced there enlarge and differentiate as they are left behind; mature stem and leaf cells do not normally divide.
items.specStatementText: Proliferation for growth, replacement and repair
items.random_wrong: Cells at the surface of the skin dividing to replace themselves as they wear away: cell replacement; cells in the meristems of a plant dividing: growth.

items.q: Which statement correctly gives the sequence of phases in the cell cycle?
items.correct: Interphase, made up of G1, S and G2 in that order, is followed by mitosis and then by cytokinesis.
items.misconception: Interphase, made up of G1 and G2, is followed by S, in which the DNA is replicated, and then by mitosis and cytokinesis.
items.why: G2 is described as 'preparation for mitosis', and copying the DNA seems the obvious preparation; the sequence G1, S, G2 is memorized without the meaning of S. The sequence of interphase is G1 (growth), S (synthesis of DNA, i.e. replication) and then G2 (further growth and preparation for mitosis). By G2 every chromosome already consists of two chromatids.
items.specStatementText: The cell cycle: G1, S, G2, mitosis, cytokinesis
items.random_wrong: Interphase, a resting period in which the cell is inactive, is followed by mitosis and then by cytokinesis.

items.q: The mass of DNA per nucleus was measured for many cells from a growing tissue. Most nuclei contained 6.0 pg, a smaller group contained 12.0 pg, and a few contained values between 6.0 and 12.0 pg. Which interpretation is correct?
items.correct: The 6.0 pg nuclei are in G1, the 12.0 pg nuclei have completed S phase and are in G2 or entering mitosis, and the intermediate values are nuclei in S phase.
items.misconception: The 12.0 pg nuclei have twice as many chromosomes as the 6.0 pg nuclei, so they belong to cells that have just completed mitosis.
items.why: Students learn that mitosis 'maintains the chromosome number' and equate chromosome number with amount of DNA. DNA is synthesized during S phase, so the mass of DNA per nucleus doubles between G1 and G2 while the number of chromosomes stays constant; each chromosome simply comes to consist of two chromatids.
items.specStatementText: Interphase is busy, not resting
items.random_wrong: The intermediate values are measurement errors, because the DNA content of a nucleus does not change during the inactivity of interphase.

items.q: The concentration of one cyclin was measured in cells passing through the cell cycle. It was low in G1, rose through S and G2, peaked as mitosis began and then fell sharply. When a chemical stopped the concentration of this cyclin from rising beyond half its usual peak, the cells remained in G2. Which conclusion is best supported?
items.correct: A threshold concentration of this cyclin must be reached to pass the checkpoint that allows the cell to enter mitosis.
items.misconception: This cyclin acts as a brake on the cycle, so the cells could not enter mitosis because its concentration had failed to fall.
items.why: 'Control' and 'checkpoint' both suggest stopping, so a control protein is imagined as a barrier rather than as a signal to proceed. A checkpoint is passed when the concentration of a specific cyclin rises above a threshold. A cell that cannot accumulate enough of that cyclin is held at the checkpoint; the cyclin is the go signal, not the brake.
items.specStatementText: Cyclins let the cell pass checkpoints
items.random_wrong: The concentration of a cyclin should rise continuously through the whole cycle, so the sharp fall shows that these cells had died.

items.q: Which statement about the control of the cell cycle by cyclins is correct?
items.correct: The concentrations of different cyclins rise and fall at different points in the cycle, and a threshold level of a specific cyclin is needed to pass each checkpoint.
items.misconception: A single cyclin increases steadily in concentration throughout the cycle, and its level at any moment tells the cell which phase it is in.
items.why: The word 'cycle' and a graph of one rising line are remembered, while the several separate curves for different cyclins are not. Cyclins are a family of proteins. The concentration of each rises and falls during the cycle, and it is a threshold level of a specific cyclin that is required to pass a specific checkpoint.
items.specStatementText: Cyclins let the cell pass checkpoints
items.random_wrong: Cyclins hold the cell at each checkpoint, and the cell passes through only when the concentration of the relevant cyclin falls below a threshold.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes how mutations in genes that control the cell cycle lead to uncontrolled cell division?
items.correct: A mutation can turn a proto-oncogene into an oncogene that drives division, or stop a tumour suppressor gene restraining division.
items.misconception: Mutations make both proto-oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes over-active, so both kinds of gene then stimulate division more strongly.
items.why: Both kinds of gene are lumped together as 'genes whose mutation causes cancer', and 'mutation causes over-activity' is the only mechanism students know. The two act in opposite directions. Converting a proto-oncogene to an oncogene is a gain of function: the product stimulates division more. A tumour suppressor mutation is a loss of function: the product that would halt division is no longer effective.
items.specStatementText: Mutations in cell-cycle genes drive uncontrolled division
items.random_wrong: An oncogene is a gene that a healthy cell does not possess, so uncontrolled division can begin only when one is introduced from outside.

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes between types of tumour?
items.correct: A malignant tumour invades neighbouring tissue and can spread to form secondary tumours; a benign tumour does neither and does not cause cancer.
items.misconception: A benign tumour is a harmless overgrowth of normal tissue, not the result of uncontrolled division, so it is not a true tumour.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'benign' is 'kindly, harmless', so students assume a benign tumour is normal tissue. Both benign and malignant tumours result from uncontrolled cell division. The difference is that a benign tumour remains in one place and does not invade or metastasize, so it does not cause cancer, although it can still cause harm by its size and position.
items.specStatementText: Benign versus malignant, and measuring the mitotic index
items.random_wrong: A secondary tumour is a second tumour that arises independently in a different tissue, from a different set of mutations.

items.q: A student examined 240 cells in a micrograph of a growing tissue. 204 cells had an intact nucleus with no visible chromosomes, and the remaining 36 cells had condensed chromosomes visible. What is the mitotic index of the sample?
items.why: Comparisons are often expressed as ratios of one group to the other, and 'dividing versus not dividing' feels like the natural comparison. The mitotic index is the fraction (or percentage) of all cells counted that are in mitosis, so the denominator is the total number of cells, including those in interphase.
items.specStatementText: Benign versus malignant, and measuring the mitotic index

items.q: The mitotic index was determined for three samples: cells from a root-tip meristem, 0.12; cells from a tumour removed from a patient, 0.10; cells from a mature leaf, 0.00. A student concluded that the tumour must be benign because its mitotic index is lower than that of a healthy meristem. Which evaluation of this conclusion is correct?
items.correct: It is not justified: the mitotic index measures how many cells are dividing, but malignancy depends on the capacity to invade tissue and metastasize.
items.misconception: It is not justified: a mitotic index as high as 0.12 shows that the meristem itself is cancerous, so it cannot serve as a healthy tissue for comparison.
items.why: Cancer is introduced as 'uncontrolled cell division', so all rapid division is read as cancer. Mitotic index measures the rate of cell division, not its control. Normal proliferating tissues have high mitotic indices, and a tumour's malignancy depends on whether its cells invade and spread, which a count of dividing cells cannot show.
items.specStatementText: Benign versus malignant, and measuring the mitotic index
items.random_wrong: It is justified: malignant tumours are defined by dividing faster than normal tissue, so a tumour dividing more slowly than a meristem is benign.

items.q: How many daughter cells does one cell division produce?
items.correct: Two.
items.misconception: A parent cell splits at one time into many small daughter cells, which then grow.
items.why: Students learn that a single fertilized egg gives rise to trillions of cells and that bacteria multiply rapidly, and they picture a cell fragmenting into many pieces; micrographs of early embryos show many cells that all seem to have appeared at once. Each cell division produces exactly two daughter cells. Large numbers of cells arise from many repeated divisions, each daughter cell dividing again in turn.
items.specStatementText: New cells only come from cells dividing
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What forms the ring that pinches an animal cell in two?
items.correct: A ring of contractile actin and myosin proteins, just inside the cell membrane.
items.misconception: The contractile ring and the spindle are the same machinery: the ring is made of the spindle's microtubules, or the spindle is made of actin and myosin, and either one can pull on membranes and chromosomes alike.
items.why: Both structures are protein fibres that appear during division, and diagrams draw both as lines, so students merge the two into one all-purpose 'fibre' system. Two separate systems are used. Spindle microtubules and microtubule motors move chromosomes; a ring of actin and myosin, the same proteins that produce contraction in muscle, pinches the membrane of an animal cell to split the cytoplasm.
items.specStatementText: Cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm, differently in animals and plants
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Could a daughter cell that received no mitochondria make some for itself?
items.correct: No. Mitochondria (and chloroplasts) are made only by growth and division of existing mitochondria, so each daughter cell must receive at least one.
items.misconception: A cell can synthesize new mitochondria or chloroplasts from scratch, using its ribosomes and nuclear genes, so organelles do not need to be shared out at division.
items.why: Students learn that ribosomes make proteins and that the nucleus controls the cell, and they extend this to the idea that a cell can build any of its structures from raw materials. Some organelles can only be produced by division of a pre-existing organelle. Mitochondria and chloroplasts are the clear examples; they contain their own DNA and grow and divide. A cell with none could not make any, so each daughter cell must receive at least one.
items.specStatementText: Cytokinesis is usually equal, but not always
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does the bud of a yeast cell obtain its nucleus?
items.correct: The nucleus of the parent cell divides by mitosis and one of the two nuclei moves into the bud before it is pinched off.
items.misconception: A yeast bud is a piece of cytoplasm that grows out and pinches off without any nuclear division, and it forms a nucleus of its own later.
items.why: The everyday word 'bud' suggests an outgrowth like a plant bud, and diagrams of budding often show the bud before a nucleus has been drawn into it. Budding is mitotic reproduction with unequal cytokinesis. The nucleus divides by mitosis, one nucleus enters the bud along with mitochondria and other organelles, and the bud is then separated from the larger parent cell.
items.specStatementText: Cytokinesis is usually equal, but not always
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is cytokinesis a phase of mitosis?
items.correct: No. Mitosis is nuclear division; cytokinesis is the separate splitting of the cytoplasm that usually follows it.
items.misconception: Cytokinesis is the final phase of mitosis, after telophase, so mitosis and cell division are the same thing.
items.why: Flow charts of the cell cycle list 'prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, cytokinesis' in one sequence, and GCSE courses describe 'the cell divides by mitosis' without separating nucleus from cytoplasm. Mitosis is the division of the nucleus and ends with two nuclei in telophase. Cytokinesis, the splitting of the cytoplasm, is a distinct process; nuclear division has to happen before it so that neither daughter cell is left without a nucleus.
items.specStatementText: Mitosis keeps the genome; meiosis halves it and adds variety
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When is the DNA of a chromosome replicated?
items.correct: During interphase, before mitosis or meiosis begins.
items.misconception: DNA is replicated during prophase, when the chromosomes are seen to change from single threads into two chromatids.
items.why: Chromosomes only become visible as two chromatids when they condense in prophase, so students assume the second chromatid is made then. DNA replication is a prerequisite for both mitosis and meiosis and takes place in interphase. By prophase each chromosome already consists of two chromatids; condensation makes the existing chromatids visible but does not copy them.
items.specStatementText: DNA is replicated once before either division
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are chromosomes condensed all the time?
items.correct: No. During interphase the DNA is extended; it is condensed only for nuclear division and decondenses again afterwards.
items.misconception: DNA is permanently packed as condensed chromosomes, which simply become visible when a dividing cell is stained.
items.why: Karyotypes and textbook diagrams show chromosomes only in their condensed, X-shaped form, so students treat that shape as the permanent state of the DNA. Condensation is a shared feature of mitosis and meiosis that occurs in prophase. Between divisions the DNA is extended so that it can be transcribed and replicated; the supercoiled chromosome is a temporary form for moving the DNA without damage.
items.specStatementText: Chromosomes condense and are moved by microtubules in both divisions
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do chromatids move apart because they repel one another?
items.correct: No. They are moved by microtubules and microtubule motor proteins attached at the centromere.
items.misconception: Once the centromere divides, the two chromatids repel each other and drift to opposite ends of the cell without being attached to anything.
items.why: Simplified anaphase diagrams often omit the spindle and just show chromatids moving apart, and the smooth symmetrical movement looks like repulsion. Movement of chromosomes in both mitosis and meiosis depends on the spindle. Motor proteins move each chromatid along microtubules towards the pole, and the microtubules shorten; without the spindle the chromatids would not separate.
items.specStatementText: Chromosomes condense and are moved by microtubules in both divisions
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the nuclear envelope present while the chromosomes move during mitosis?
items.correct: No. It breaks down in prophase and re-forms around each set of chromosomes in telophase.
items.misconception: The nuclear envelope stays intact throughout mitosis and the chromosomes line up and separate inside it.
items.why: Diagrams draw a circle around the cell and often a second one around the chromosomes, and students who think of the nucleus as a permanent organelle assume it simply divides in two. In prophase the nuclear envelope breaks down so that spindle microtubules from the poles can reach the chromosomes. Only in telophase, when the two sets of chromosomes have reached the poles, do new nuclear envelopes form around them.
items.specStatementText: The four phases of mitosis
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which phase follows metaphase?
items.correct: Anaphase, in which the sister chromatids are separated and moved to opposite poles.
items.misconception: The names metaphase and anaphase are swapped: 'anaphase' is when the chromosomes are arranged across the middle and 'metaphase' is when they move apart.
items.why: Both names are unfamiliar Greek prefixes learned as a list (PMAT); the order is memorized but the meanings are not, so the two middle names are easily exchanged. Metaphase (meta = middle) is when the chromosomes are lined up on the equator; anaphase (ana = apart) is when the chromatids are moved apart towards the poles.
items.specStatementText: Reading the phase from a diagram or micrograph
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many nuclear divisions take place in meiosis?
items.correct: Two: meiosis I and meiosis II, producing four haploid nuclei from one diploid nucleus.
items.misconception: Meiosis is a single division that halves the chromosome number, producing two haploid cells.
items.why: Students remember the outcome 'halves the chromosome number' and, since mitosis is one division, assume one halving division is all that is needed. Meiosis involves two rounds of segregation: homologous chromosomes are separated in meiosis I and sister chromatids in meiosis II. The result is four haploid nuclei, not two.
items.specStatementText: Meiosis: two divisions, one diploid nucleus to four haploid
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: At what stage does the extra chromosome 21 arise?
items.correct: During meiosis in one parent, when chromosomes 21 (or their chromatids) fail to separate and both go into the same gamete.
items.misconception: The extra chromosome arises at fertilization, when the sperm and egg fuse and an additional chromosome 21 is produced.
items.why: The affected individual is the zygote, so students locate the error at the moment the zygote forms rather than earlier, in the formation of the gametes. Non-disjunction is an error of meiosis: a homologous pair fails to separate in anaphase I, or sister chromatids fail to separate in anaphase II. The gamete already carries two copies of chromosome 21 before fertilization adds a third.
items.specStatementText: Non-disjunction and Down syndrome
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When non-disjunction produces a gamete with an extra chromosome, what about the other gamete from that division?
items.correct: It lacks that chromosome altogether, so it has one fewer than the normal number.
items.misconception: Only one gamete is affected by non-disjunction; the others from the same division are normal.
items.why: Diagrams and examples focus on the gamete with the extra chromosome and the trisomy it produces, and the gamete that lost the chromosome is rarely shown. Non-disjunction sends both copies to one pole and none to the other, so one gamete has an extra chromosome and another is missing it. A zygote formed from the second kind lacks one chromosome of the pair and usually cannot develop.
items.specStatementText: Non-disjunction and Down syndrome
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does 'random orientation' of bivalents mean?
items.correct: Each bivalent lines up on the equator with its maternal or its paternal chromosome facing a given pole at random, independently of the other bivalents; every gamete still gets one chromosome of each pair.
items.misconception: Random orientation means the chromosomes are shared out at random, so gametes receive different numbers of chromosomes, or a random selection that may lack some.
items.why: The word 'random' suggests that nothing is fixed, and students who have not grasped that homologues pair before separating assume the whole set is dealt out haphazardly. What is random is only which member of each pair goes to which pole. Because the homologues of each bivalent go to opposite poles, every gamete receives exactly one chromosome of every type; the combination of maternal and paternal chromosomes differs from gamete to gamete.
items.specStatementText: Meiosis makes variation: random orientation and crossing over
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does crossing over produce new alleles?
items.correct: No. It produces new combinations of the alleles already present on the two homologous chromosomes.
items.misconception: Crossing over changes the base sequence at the point of exchange, creating new alleles and so new variation.
items.why: 'Source of variation' and 'new combinations' are heard as 'new genes', and mutation, the actual source of new alleles, is taught in the same unit. Crossing over exchanges corresponding lengths of DNA between homologues, so the genes and alleles are the same afterwards but are arranged in new combinations on each chromatid. New alleles arise only by mutation.
items.specStatementText: Meiosis makes variation: random orientation and crossing over
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are crossing over and random orientation the same process?
items.correct: No. Crossing over is an exchange of DNA between non-sister chromatids in prophase I; random orientation is the chance arrangement of bivalents on the equator at metaphase I.
items.misconception: Crossing over and random orientation are the same thing: crossing over decides which chromosome of each pair goes to which pole.
items.why: Both are introduced together as 'ways meiosis creates variation', and both are summarized loosely as 'the chromosomes get mixed up'. Meiosis generates diversity in two separate ways. Crossing over recombines alleles within a chromosome; random orientation of bivalents recombines whole maternal and paternal chromosomes. They occur at different stages and are independent of each other.
items.specStatementText: Meiosis makes variation: random orientation and crossing over
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is the gap left by a skin wound filled?
items.correct: Cells at the edges of the wound proliferate by repeated cell cycles, producing new cells that cover the gap.
items.misconception: The existing cells around a wound stretch and enlarge until they fill the gap.
items.why: Skin visibly stretches, and 'the wound closes' sounds like a purely mechanical event; cell division is invisible to the eye. Wound healing in skin is an example of cell proliferation for tissue repair. Cells near the wound re-enter the cell cycle and divide repeatedly, and the new cells replace those that were lost.
items.specStatementText: Proliferation for growth, replacement and repair
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which skin cells divide to replace those shed from the surface?
items.correct: Cells beneath the surface proliferate; the new cells move outwards and replace those shed from the surface.
items.misconception: The cells at the surface of the skin divide to replace themselves as they wear away.
items.why: Students assume that replacement happens where the loss occurs, at the surface itself. Routine cell replacement in skin depends on proliferation of cells beneath the surface. Cells produced there are pushed outwards, replacing the cells that are continually lost from the surface.
items.specStatementText: Proliferation for growth, replacement and repair
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which part of the cell cycle takes most of the time?
items.correct: Interphase (G1, S and G2); mitosis and cytokinesis are a relatively short part of the cycle.
items.misconception: Mitosis occupies most of the cell cycle, with interphase a brief gap between divisions.
items.why: Mitosis is taught in detail with four named phases while interphase is a single word, so its share of the cycle is imagined to be correspondingly large. Interphase occupies most of the cycle: the cell grows, replicates its DNA and prepares for division. Mitosis is short, which is why in a micrograph of a growing tissue most cells show an interphase nucleus.
items.specStatementText: The cell cycle: G1, S, G2, mitosis, cytokinesis
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is interphase a resting stage?
items.correct: No. It is metabolically very active: the cell grows by synthesizing proteins and other components, replicates its DNA and increases its organelles.
items.misconception: Interphase is a resting phase in which nothing much happens while the cell waits to divide again.
items.why: The name 'interphase' means 'between phases', and under the microscope an interphase cell looks static compared with the dramatic movements of mitosis. Interphase is the period of growth and biosynthesis. Proteins are made throughout it, DNA is replicated in S phase, and mitochondria (and chloroplasts) grow and divide so that their numbers increase before the cell divides.
items.specStatementText: Interphase is busy, not resting
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to a cyclin's concentration after its checkpoint has been passed?
items.correct: It falls again, so the checkpoint cannot be passed a second time until the concentration has built up once more.
items.misconception: Once a cyclin has reached the threshold for its checkpoint it stays at that high level for the rest of the cycle.
items.why: Students picture the checkpoint as a switch that is thrown once, and do not notice that the graph of cyclin concentration comes back down. Cyclin concentrations both increase and decrease during the cycle. After the threshold has been reached and the checkpoint passed, the cyclin concentration falls, which is part of what makes the cycle a cycle.
items.specStatementText: Cyclins let the cell pass checkpoints
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an oncogene something a healthy cell already possesses?
items.correct: A healthy cell possesses proto-oncogenes, normal genes that promote the cell cycle; a mutation converts a proto-oncogene into an oncogene.
items.misconception: Oncogenes are foreign 'cancer genes' that normal cells do not have; they have to be introduced from outside by a virus or a carcinogen.
items.why: The name 'oncogene' sounds like a gene for cancer, and carcinogens and viruses are known causes of cancer, so students assume the gene itself must come from the cause. Proto-oncogenes are normal genes that control cell division. A mutation, whatever causes it, can convert a proto-oncogene into an oncogene whose product drives division without the usual controls.
items.specStatementText: Mutations in cell-cycle genes drive uncontrolled division
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the mutations that cause a tumour passed on to the next generation?
items.correct: Usually not: they arise in body (somatic) cells, so they affect only the individual in which they occur.
items.misconception: Mutations in cell-cycle control genes happen in the gametes, so the resulting uncontrolled division appears in the offspring that inherit them.
items.why: In the genetics course mutations are studied through their inheritance, so all mutations are assumed to be passed on. Most mutations that convert proto-oncogenes to oncogenes or disable tumour suppressor genes occur in somatic cells during the life of an individual. The affected cell divides uncontrollably to form a tumour in that individual; such mutations are not in the gametes and are not inherited.
items.specStatementText: Mutations in cell-cycle genes drive uncontrolled division
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is a secondary tumour?
items.correct: A tumour formed elsewhere in the body by cells that detached from a malignant primary tumour and spread (metastasis).
items.misconception: A secondary tumour is a second tumour that arises independently in another tissue, from its own mutations, later in life.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'secondary' is 'second' or 'less important', so a secondary tumour is heard as 'another one'. A secondary tumour is a consequence of metastasis: cells from the primary tumour travel, often in the blood or lymph, and establish a tumour in a new site. It consists of the same type of cell as the primary tumour.
items.specStatementText: Benign versus malignant, and measuring the mitotic index
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What distinguishes a malignant tumour from a benign one?
items.correct: Its capacity to invade neighbouring tissue and to metastasize to other parts of the body.
items.misconception: Malignant tumours are the ones that grow faster and larger; size and growth rate define whether a tumour is malignant.
items.why: Tumours differ in their rates of division and growth, and cancer is associated with rapid growth, so growth rate is taken as the defining feature. Rates of cell division and growth vary among tumours of both kinds. The defining feature of a malignant tumour is invasion of neighbouring tissue and the capacity for metastasis; a large or fast-growing tumour is not necessarily malignant.
items.specStatementText: Benign versus malignant, and measuring the mitotic index
